interactions.label: ρ (Distance)
interactions.teaches: Scaling ρ changes the point's distance from the origin, lengthening the blue segment while the angles θ and φ remain locked.

interactions.label: θ (Azimuth)
interactions.teaches: Changing θ rotates the entire construction around the z-axis, sweeping the projection r across the xy-plane.

interactions.label: φ (Zenith)
interactions.teaches: Changing φ tilts the ρ segment away from the vertical z-axis. As φ increases, P drops closer to the xy-plane, decreasing z and increasing r.

demo_steps.title: Unified View
demo_steps.narration: A single point P can be described by rectangular (x,y,z), cylindrical (r,θ,z), or spherical (ρ,θ,φ) coordinates simultaneously.

demo_steps.title: Varying Zenith Angle
demo_steps.narration: Increasing φ lowers the point. Watch how the vertical drop z shrinks while the radial shadow r grows, even as ρ stays constant.

demo_steps.title: Varying Azimuth Angle
demo_steps.narration: Changing θ sweeps the point around the z-axis. The distance ρ and height z remain unchanged, highlighting how spherical and cylindrical systems share θ.

plan.geometry_notes: Use a Z-up math coordinate system. Axes span 0 to 10. CRITICAL: Axis labels (x, y, z) must use a large font size and be positioned with enough offset from the axis tips to prevent clipping at the screen edges. The label for Point P must be fixed, static text: 'P(x, y, z)' and 'P(ρ, θ, φ)'; do NOT inject dynamic numbers into these strings. The ρ segment is solid blue #1f4e79. Drop z, radial r, and xy-plane projections are dashed orange #cc5500. Point P is a black sphere radius 0.2. All components must be visible simultaneously. Derived values for geometry positioning: x = ρ*sin(φ)*cos(θ), y = ρ*sin(φ)*sin(θ), z = ρ*cos(φ), r = ρ*sin(φ).
plan.notes: Recompute line endpoints, arc paths, and dependent text label positions in a reactive loop when sliders change. Use THREE.LineDashedMaterial for the orange segments and ensure computeLineDistances() is called dynamically so the dashes render correctly throughout the animation.

authoredPrompt: This figure is a three-dimensional construction drawn in the first octant that locates a single point three different ways at once. The vertical axis is labeled z, the axis running to the right is labeled y, and the axis coming toward the viewer at the lower left is labeled x. A filled black dot at the upper right is tagged by two stacked lines of text, P(x, y, z) on top and P(rho, theta, phi) beneath it. A solid blue segment runs from the origin out to the dot and is labeled rho along its length. A small arc near the origin between the z-axis and that segment is labeled phi. Dashed orange lines complete the rest of the construction: a vertical drop from the point down to the xy-plane labeled z, and a segment from the origin across the xy-plane to the foot of that drop labeled r, with a small square where they meet marking the right angle. A second arc at the origin, between the x-axis and the segment r, is labeled theta. Superimposing all three descriptions on one point exposes theta and r as the quantities the systems share. The drawing introduces the ordered triple (rho, theta, phi), in which one distance and two angles fix a location in space.
authoredInteractions:
- Slider for rho, theta, and phi: the learner adjusts each coordinate, the point P moves while the radial segment, ground projection, vertical height, and angle arcs update, showing how one distance and two angles determine a 3D location.
- Toggle between rectangular, cylindrical, and spherical readouts: the learner switches coordinate systems, the same point remains fixed while x,y,z, r,theta,z, and rho,theta,phi components highlight, making clear which quantities are shared and which are system-specific.
authoredContext:
In the spherical coordinate system, a point P in space (the figure) is represented by the ordered triple (ρ,θ,φ) where

In the Cartesian coordinate system, the location of a point in space is described using an ordered triple in which each coordinate represents a distance. In the cylindrical coordinate system, location of a point in space is described using two distances (randz) and an angle measure (θ). In the spherical coordinate system, we again use an ordered triple to describe the location of a point in space. In this case, the triple describes one distance and two angles. Spherical coordinates make it simple to describe a sphere, just as cylindrical coordinates make it easy to describe a cylinder. Grid lines for spherical coordinates are based on angle measures, like those for polar coordinates.

The relationship among spherical, rectangular, and cylindrical coordinates.

This figure is the first quadrant of the 3-dimensional coordinate system. It has a point labeled “(x, y, z) = (rho, theta, phi).” There is a line segment from the origin to the point. It is labeled “rho.” The angle between this line segment and the z-axis is phi. There is a line segment in the x y-plane from the origin to the shadow of the point. This segment is labeled “r.” The angle between the x-axis and r is theta.

By convention, the origin is represented as (0,0,0) in spherical coordinates.
sourceQmd: OpenStax Calculus, chapter 12: Vectors in Space

Point P as a filled black dot
Solid blue segment from origin to P (ρ)
Dashed orange vertical segment from P down to its projection on the xy-plane (z)

interactions.label: ρ (Distance)
interactions.teaches: Changing ρ scales the point's distance from the origin, moving it along the radial line without altering its angular direction.

interactions.label: θ (Azimuth)
interactions.teaches: Changing θ rotates the point around the z-axis, sweeping its shadow (r) across the xy-plane.

interactions.label: φ (Zenith)
interactions.teaches: Changing φ tilts the point away from the vertical z-axis. Increasing it lowers the point toward the xy-plane.

interactions.label: Coordinate System
interactions.teaches: Highlights the specific geometric components (distances and angles) used to define the same point's location in different coordinate systems.

demo_steps.title: Spherical Coordinates
demo_steps.narration: In the spherical system, P is located by its distance from the origin (ρ) and two angles: θ from the x-axis and φ from the z-axis.

demo_steps.title: Cylindrical Coordinates
demo_steps.narration: Switching to cylindrical, the vertical height z is used alongside the polar coordinates (r, θ) of the point's shadow on the xy-plane.

demo_steps.title: Rectangular Coordinates
demo_steps.narration: In rectangular coordinates, the location is defined purely by orthogonal distances x, y, and z along the three axes.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Use a Z-up math coordinate system (map Three.y = Math.z, Three.x = Math.y, Three.z = Math.x). Axes span 0 to 10. ρ segment is solid blue #1f4e79. Drop z, radial r, and xy-plane projections (x, y) are dashed orange #cc5500. Point P is a black sphere radius 0.15. Arcs are thin black lines. Right angle marker is a small square (0.4 units side) at the junction of r and z. Highlight logic based on toggle: Spherical shows ρ, φ, θ; Cylindrical shows r, θ, z; Rectangular shows x, y, z (hide unused dashed lines and labels). Calculate derived values: x = ρ*sin(φ)*cos(θ), y = ρ*sin(φ)*sin(θ), z = ρ*cos(φ), r = ρ*sin(φ).
interactionPlan.notes: Ensure text labels for the point update dynamically to show P(ρ, θ, φ), P(r, θ, z), or P(x, y, z) depending on the active toggle state. Use THREE.LineDashedMaterial for dashed segments and ensure line distances are computed so the dashes render correctly. Recompute all dependent geometry and label positions in a reactive loop when sliders change.

Draw the right-angle marker using the same dashed orange material as the r and z projection lines.
